name: ScyllaDB
workload: ScyllaDB's own cassandra-stress comparison of ScyllaDB 4.4.3 against Apache Cassandra 4.0: equal 3-node clusters of AWS i3.4xlarge, maximum throughput while P99 latency stays under 10 ms, plus a '4 vs 40' test of 4 i3.metal ScyllaDB nodes against 40 i3.4xlarge Cassandra nodes with fifteen loader machines.
claimed_speedup: Vendor claim (search-result text only, page not opened): 3x-8x the throughput of Cassandra 4.0 on equal 3-node clusters at P99 under 10 ms (white-paper table range 2.66x-8x); 4 ScyllaDB i3.metal nodes give 42% more throughput than 40 Cassandra i3.4xlarge nodes at P99 under 10 ms and cost 2.5x less for a 40 TB cluster; Cassandra 4.0 P99 latencies are 80% to 2,200% higher than ScyllaDB 4.4; a New Stack summary of the same tests gives 2x to 4.5x. The repository README itself only claims 'order-of-magnitude performance improvements' with no figures.
hardware: AWS i3.4xlarge (3-node clusters) and i3.metal (4 ScyllaDB nodes) against 40 x i3.4xlarge for Cassandra, per search-result text; CPU model and OS tuning not seen.
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing, thread-per-core design on the Seastar framework (C++23) that wants whole machines and shard-aware clients; Cassandra (CQL) and DynamoDB (Alternator) API-compatible, so a wide-column/NoSQL store with no joins and only lightweight transactions. Current licence is source-available (ScyllaDB Software License Agreement v1.1, last updated April 12 2026): limited to 'Never Customers', capped at 10 TB storage and 50 vCPUs in total, no SaaS/DBaaS use and no competing use, modifications are assigned to the licensor. Not an OSI licence, so the code is a reference, not copyable.
caveats: Snippet only: scylladb.com, resources.scylladb.com, thenewstack.io and planetcassandra.org did not resolve from this container (ENOTFOUND), so no benchmark page was opened; the figures come from WebSearch result text that repeated them consistently across two queries, and they could not be checked against the pages. Vendor-run (first-party), 2021, ScyllaDB 4.4.3 against Cassandra 4.0; the benchmarked 'Scylla Open Source 4.4' predates the current source-available licence (its licence was not checked). The harness is not in the scylladb/scylladb repo (only the cassandra-stress parameters are described in the vendor text, not seen); no compiler or flags apply to the Java baseline; no independent replication found. The '4 vs 40' test mixes cluster sizes and instance types, and the vendor itself says Cassandra 4.0 on 40 i3.4xlarge nodes has better latency at low throughput. The 3x-8x headline rounds up the table's 2.66x lower bound. Nothing in the repo (README, docs/ listing, issue #649 which only links a 2016 YCSB post) carries numbers. Category 'columnar-analytics' is the assigned guess; ScyllaDB is a distributed wide-column OLTP store, so the category fits poorly.

name: Varnish Cache
baseline: NGINX 1.12.2 proxy_cache (worker_processes 1 and worker_processes auto on 12 cores) in front of an nginx origin
workload: wrk -t 100 -c 1000 -d 30 requests for cached static files of 12 B to 1 KB through each cache server (Varnish 4.1.8 malloc 1024M, default threads; nginx 1.12.2 proxy_cache) on a 12-core Xeon, over a 1 Gbps link and over loopback, plus 5000 connections on loopback; measured by the author of the competing nuster cache.
claimed_speedup: Not a win on equal footing. Table 1 (1 Gbps, 1000 connections), requests/s: hello-world 12 B Varnish 133094 vs nginx 1 worker 33454 (3.98x, derived from page data) but vs nginx 12 workers 214217 (Varnish 0.62x, derived); 1 KB Varnish 87772 vs nginx 1 worker 36034 (2.44x, derived) and vs nginx 12 workers 91497 (0.96x, derived). Loopback, 1000 connections, hello-world: Varnish 115928 vs nginx 1 worker 30996 (3.74x, derived) and vs nginx 12 workers 136844 (0.85x, derived). Varnish is below nginx with all cores in every row of all three tables. No number against an origin server without a cache was found, and Varnish publishes no figures in its README.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: distribution packages are implied; Varnish VCL backend, beresp.ttl = 1d, VARNISH_STORAGE malloc,1024M; nginx proxy_cache STATIC, proxy_cache_valid any 1d, worker_connections 1000000, keepalive_requests 100000; wrk 4.0.2-2-g91655b5.
hardware: Intel Xeon X5650 @ 2.67GHz, 12 cores, 32 GB RAM, 1 Gbps NIC, CentOS 7.4.1708 (origin nginx on a second machine in the 1 Gbps runs)
tradeoffs: In-memory (malloc) or file-backed HTTP reverse-proxy cache configured through the VCL language, which gives fine control over caching and request handling but has a learning curve; no TLS termination in the core (needs Hitch or similar); multi-threaded, so a hit costs more cores than one nginx worker; a miss path adds latency (Varnish issue #1923 reported about 30-40 ms extra on misses with 4.0.2, snippet only).
caveats: The only numeric comparison found is a competitor's wiki page (nuster author), undated (sample output November 2017, page last edited August 2018) and on old releases (Varnish 4.1.8, nginx 1.12.2); not a first-party Varnish claim and not peer reviewed, so tier C. The only wins are against a single nginx worker (an asymmetric baseline against a multi-threaded Varnish); nginx on 12 workers beats Varnish in every row, and Varnish logged socket timeouts in two rows (17 at 1 KB in Table 1, 118 at hello-world in Table 2). Varnish's thread settings were left at defaults. The origin-without-cache baseline in the assignment has no number anywhere reachable (a varnish/hitch issue reports about 10,835 req/s through Varnish against 776 req/s through a TLS path, which is not an origin comparison). The GitHub repository was archived on 2026-02-16 and its README says development moved to code.vinyl-cache.org (that site did not resolve from this container, so it was not checked); maintenance_status is 'unknown' for that reason. Related prior work: the AdaptSize paper tunes Varnish admission and reports hit-ratio gains over stock Varnish, which is not a comparison against Varnish as the winner.

name: YugabyteDB
baseline: Apache Cassandra 3.11.1 (YCQL API against CQL, YCSB); not the assigned single-node PostgreSQL
workload: Vendor 2017 YCSB comparison of YugaByte DB's Cassandra-compatible YCQL API against Apache Cassandra 3.11.1 on 3-node clusters (replication factor 3) at 1 million and 10 million keys; the original post's exact instance type was not seen.
claimed_speedup: Vendor claim (search-result text only, page not opened): workload A about 74,710 ops/s for Cassandra vs 90,520 for YugaByte DB (1.21x, derived from those figures); workload C about 72,873 vs 103,484 (1.42x, derived); on the 100% read workload about 42% faster than Cassandra at 1 million keys and 95% faster at 10 million keys, and ahead on p99 latency too. No figure against single-node PostgreSQL favours YugabyteDB; see caveats for the opposite results.
hardware: Described in the search text as 3 nodes on Google Cloud; machine type and CPU model not seen.
tradeoffs: Distributed SQL database: DocDB storage layer in C++ with Raft replication, a forked PostgreSQL query layer (YSQL) and a Cassandra-style API (YCQL). Pays for strong consistency and horizontal scale with extra network round trips, so single-node latency and throughput trail plain PostgreSQL and Cassandra in independent tests. The default build produces only Apache-2.0 binaries; the managed/ directory (YugabyteDB Anywhere) is under the Polyform Free Trial licence 1.0.0 and is not OSI. The assigned category columnar-analytics fits poorly: this is a distributed OLTP database.
caveats: Snippet only: forum.yugabyte.com, yugabyte.com and docs.yugabyte.com did not resolve from this container (ENOTFOUND), so the vendor figures come from one WebSearch result summary and were not corroborated; the second search confirmed only that the vendor posts claim a throughput and p99 lead that grows with key count. Vendor-run, 2017, Cassandra 3.11.1, with a Cassandra configuration tuned by the vendor in the follow-up post. Opposite independent evidence was opened: MaibornWolff/database-performance-comparison (Apache-2.0, YugabyteDB 2.15.0 on 3 x i3.8xlarge, IoT insert workload) reports YSQL 295,000 inserts/s against single-instance PostgreSQL 428,000, YCQL 288,000 against Cassandra 389,000 (sync) and 410,000 (async), and YSQL query times 160 s vs 39 s (count-events), 1700 s vs 119 s (temperature-stats-per-device), with newest-per-device failing; so YugabyteDB is slower than both assigned and Cassandra baselines there. The repo's own docs (docs/content/stable/benchmark/, faq/comparisons/cassandra.md and postgresql.md) give YugabyteDB-only numbers or qualitative comparisons, with no head-to-head figures; README says only 'PostgreSQL-like performance' for the cost-based optimizer. Search snippets also mention user issues reporting YSQL far slower than PostgreSQL on single-node workloads (snippet only).
